description: Al-Qadr (predestination and free will), Akhirah (life after death), Barzakh, al-Jannah and Jahannam.
content_html:
Al-Qadr: The Divine Masterplan

One of the most thought-provoking Islamic beliefs is al-Qadr, often translated as predestination or the divine masterplan. Islam teaches that Allah is all-knowing — His knowledge extends to everything that has happened, is happening, and will happen. The Qur’an expresses this in Surah al-Ahzab (33:38): “And ever is the command of Allah a destiny decreed.” This does not mean that Allah causes evil or forces people to sin; rather, it means that nothing in creation falls outside His knowledge or control.

The concept of sifat (Allah’s attributes) is relevant here. Because Allah’s knowledge (Al-‘Alim) is eternal and infinite, He knows every choice every person will make before they make it. This is sometimes called Allah’s foreknowledge. However, Muslims emphasise that Allah’s foreknowing a choice does not force the person to make it: the person still chooses freely, and Allah’s knowledge simply reflects that choice. Surah Yusuf (12:42) illustrates the tension between divine decree and human agency through the story of Yusuf, whose life involved betrayal, imprisonment and eventual triumph — all part of a divine plan that unfolded through human decisions.

Free Will and Human Responsibility

The relationship between al-Qadr and free will is one of the most discussed questions in Islamic philosophy. Most Muslims hold that both are true simultaneously: Allah has foreknowledge of all events, and human beings genuinely choose their actions and are held accountable for them on the Day of Judgement. The Qur’an insists on human responsibility: “Every soul, for what it has earned, will be held in pledge” (Surah al-Muddathir 74:38, which is associated with the section on accountability cited in the plan for al-Ma’ad).

The question of how to reconcile divine foreknowledge with human freedom produced two major schools of Islamic thought. The Mu’tazilite school (active from roughly the 8th to 10th centuries) emphasised human free will. They argued that if Allah predestined every human action, then it would be unjust to punish people for sins they could not avoid. Since Allah is perfectly just, the Mu’tazilites concluded that human beings must have genuine freedom of choice.

The Al-Ash’ari school, founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash’ari (874–936 CE), became the dominant Sunni theological position. Al-Ash’ari theologians taught that Allah’s decree encompasses all events, but that humans “acquire” (kasb) their actions — meaning they are morally responsible even though Allah is the ultimate originator of all things. This preserves both divine sovereignty and human accountability, though it requires accepting a degree of mystery in how exactly the two coexist. Most Shi’a theologians, influenced by Mu’tazilite thought, have tended to place a stronger emphasis on human freedom as a corollary of divine justice (Al-Adl).

Akhirah: Life After Death

Akhirah is the Islamic term for the afterlife. It is one of the six Sunni articles of faith and the fifth Shi’a Root of Usul ad-Din (Al-Ma’ad). Islam teaches that this life is only a preparation for what comes next: every action, word, thought and intention is being recorded, and on the Day of Judgement each soul will face a full and perfectly just accounting before Allah. The Qur’an frames this life as a trust and a test: “We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient” (Surah al-Baqarah 2:155).

The belief in Akhirah is inseparable from the Islamic concept of stewardship. Because every person is accountable to Allah for how they have lived, Muslims are motivated to be responsible stewards of the earth, fair in their dealings, and compassionate towards others. The afterlife belief is not merely about personal salvation but about the moral seriousness of every human choice.

Barzakh: The Interval Between Death and Judgement

Barzakh is the period between an individual’s death and the Day of Judgement. The Arabic word means “barrier” or “partition.” Islamic teachings describe Barzakh as a state of waiting in which the soul is aware of its condition but cannot return to the world of the living. The exact nature of Barzakh is not described in detail in the Qur’an, but Islamic tradition teaches that it is a real state of existence — neither full paradise nor full punishment, but a foretaste depending on the individual’s deeds. Surah al-Isra (17:49-51) touches on the question of resurrection, asking those who deny it how the dead could possibly be brought back, and asserting that Allah has the power to do so.

Key Fact

Barzakh is the intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgement. It is described as a barrier between the world of the living and the afterlife. The soul remains conscious during Barzakh but cannot return to the world. It is a waiting period, not a permanent state of reward or punishment.

The Day of Judgement

On the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din or Yawm al-Qiyamah), all souls will be resurrected and brought before Allah. Surah al-Qari’ah (Surah 101) describes the Day of Judgement as a time when “the mountains will be like wool” and the earth is transformed — powerful imagery conveying the magnitude of the event. Each person’s book of deeds will be opened: those whose scale of good deeds is heavy will enter paradise; those whose scale is light will face punishment. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to signal the beginning of this event.

Al-Jannah and Jahannam

Al-Jannah (paradise) is described in the Qur’an using rich and vivid imagery: gardens, flowing rivers, shade, fruit, and the ultimate reward of being in the presence of Allah. It is not simply a place of pleasure but of spiritual fulfilment and closeness to God. Jahannam (hell) is described as a place of fire and suffering, experienced by those who died in rejection of Allah or in unrepented serious sin.

Muslims disagree about whether descriptions of al-Jannah and Jahannam should be read literally or metaphorically. Some scholars, particularly in more traditional and Sunni circles, take the descriptions at face value — there are real gardens, real rivers, real fire. Other scholars, especially those influenced by Sufi or philosophical approaches, understand the imagery as pointing to spiritual realities that cannot be fully expressed in human language. Both positions are found within mainstream Islamic scholarship.

Martyrdom has a special place in Islamic eschatology. Classical Islamic theology teaches that those who die as martyrs in the path of Allah (shahid) are believed to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise immediately, without waiting for the Day of Judgement. This belief has been interpreted in very different ways — from those who see martyrdom only in the context of self-defence or just war, to extremist interpretations that have been widely condemned by mainstream Muslim scholars as distortions of the tradition.

Key Fact

Al-Jannah (paradise) is the eternal reward of the righteous — a state of spiritual fulfilment and closeness to Allah, described in vivid imagery including gardens and rivers. Jahannam (hell) is the place of punishment for those who rejected Allah. Surah 101 (al-Qari’ah) vividly depicts the Day of Judgement when all will be held to account, connecting eschatology to the theme of moral responsibility that runs throughout Islamic belief.
exam_tip_html: The predestination topic (al-Qadr) is one of the most nuanced in this unit. Examiners reward students who go beyond simply saying “Muslims believe in fate” and instead explain the Mu’tazilite vs Al-Ash’ari debate, or the tension between divine foreknowledge and human freedom. For Barzakh, make sure you can distinguish it clearly from both death itself and from the final afterlife state — it is the ‘in between.’ For a 15-mark Discuss question on life after death, argue both that literal interpretations reinforce moral seriousness and that metaphorical interpretations may better capture the ineffable nature of the divine. Cite Surah 2:155 (testing), Surah 33:38 (destiny), Surah 101 (Day of Judgement). SPaG marks reward correct spelling: ‘al-Qadr’, ‘Akhirah’, ‘Barzakh’, ‘Jahannam’, ‘Mu’tazilite’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Al-Qadr is the belief that Allah has foreknowledge and a divine masterplan for all creation; humans still choose freely and are accountable. The Mu’tazilite school stressed free will; the Al-Ash’ari school stressed divine sovereignty while preserving human responsibility through the concept of ‘acquisition’ (kasb).
  • Akhirah (the afterlife) is central to Islamic ethics: life is a preparation and a test, and every action is recorded. Barzakh is the intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgement — a barrier separating the dead from the living.
  • On the Day of Judgement, souls will be resurrected and sent to al-Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). These can be understood literally or metaphorically; martyrs are believed by many Muslims to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise immediately.

practice_questions.marks: Barzakh is the intermediate state / period between death and the Day of Judgement. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Islamic belief in Akhirah.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: Akhirah is the Islamic concept of the afterlife — the eternal existence that follows death and the Day of Judgement (1 mark); Muslims believe that this life is a preparation for Akhirah, where each soul will be judged by Allah for their deeds and sent to either al-Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline two different Muslim views on the relationship between predestination (al-Qadr) and human free will.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: the Mu'tazilite school strongly emphasised human free will, arguing that predestination without freedom would make divine punishment unjust (1 mark); the Al-Ash'ari school held that Allah's foreknowledge and power encompass all events, but that humans 'acquire' responsibility for their choices (1 mark); most Muslims accept that both divine foreknowledge and human accountability are true simultaneously, with the precise relationship remaining a mystery (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the belief in Akhirah might affect the life of a Muslim today.
practice_questions.marks: Possible points: Belief in Akhirah encourages Muslims to live ethically because every action is recorded and will be judged — the Qur'an (2:155) describes this life as a test, motivating perseverance and moral seriousness (1+1 mark). The belief in al-Jannah and Jahannam as real consequences provides motivation to pray, give to charity and avoid serious sin — not merely out of social pressure but from genuine awareness of accountability before Allah (1+1 mark). The concept of stewardship (khalifa on earth) linked to Akhirah encourages environmental responsibility because humans will be accountable for how they treated Allah's creation (1+1 mark). Belief in Barzakh means Muslims regard death not as an end but as a transition, which can bring comfort in grief and reduce the fear of death (1+1 mark). [6 marks: 3 marks per way — 1 for a simple point, 2 for development, 3 for development with a relevant source of wisdom and authority]

practice_questions.text: 'Descriptions of heaven and hell in Islam should be interpreted literally, not metaphorically.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Qur'an describes al-Jannah and Jahannam in concrete, specific terms — gardens, rivers, fire — suggesting literal reality; many classical scholars and traditional Muslim communities take these descriptions at face value; treating them as metaphor might undermine their moral force and the seriousness of divine reward and punishment; Surah 101 describes cosmic events in graphic language, implying physical reality. Arguments against: Allah is beyond human comprehension, so descriptions of the unseen (ghayb) must necessarily use human language as an approximation; Sufi and philosophical traditions have long read these as metaphors for spiritual states of closeness to or distance from Allah; the Qur'an itself uses simile and parable throughout, suggesting not all imagery is literal; both interpretations are found within mainstream scholarship, suggesting neither is definitively required. Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Surah 101, Surah 2:155, Surah 17:49-51), reference to Sufi or philosophical vs traditional perspectives, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with sourcing; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or limited sourcing. Emerging: Brief, unsupported. [15 marks: SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: State what Muslim theology teaches about the fate of a martyr (shahid) after death.
practice_questions.marks: A martyr is believed to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise (al-Jannah) immediately. [1 mark]

knowledge_checks.q: Which school of Islamic theology placed the strongest emphasis on human free will, arguing that predestination without freedom would be unjust?
The Islamic concept of the afterlife is called _____.
Surah _____ is associated with vivid imagery of the Day of Judgement, when 'the mountains will be like wool'.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: The divine masterplan — Allah's foreknowledge of all events
Paradise — the eternal reward of the righteous
Hell — the place of punishment for those who rejected Allah

flashcard_questions.a: Predestination — the belief that Allah has foreknowledge of all events as part of His divine masterplan.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'sifat' refer to in Islamic theology?
flashcard_questions.a: The divine attributes of Allah, including His eternal foreknowledge of all events.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Mu'tazilite school believe about free will?
flashcard_questions.a: That humans have genuine freedom of choice, because predestining sin would contradict divine justice.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Al-Ash'ari school teach about predestination and responsibility?
flashcard_questions.a: That Allah's decree encompasses all things, but humans 'acquire' moral responsibility for their choices.
The Islamic concept of the afterlife — the eternal existence following death and the Day of Judgement.
The intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgement — a barrier separating the dead from the living.
Paradise — the eternal reward of the righteous after the Day of Judgement.
Hell — the place of punishment for those who rejected Allah and died unrepentant.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Surah describes the Day of Judgement when 'the mountains will be like wool'?
What is the Islamic concept of stewardship, and how does it relate to Akhirah?
flashcard_questions.a: Humans are trustees of Allah's creation; belief in Akhirah motivates responsible stewardship because all actions are judged.

flashcard_questions.q: What is believed to happen to a Muslim martyr (shahid) after death?
flashcard_questions.a: They are believed to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise immediately.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Surah al-Baqarah (2:155) connect to the belief in Akhirah?
flashcard_questions.a: It describes this life as a test — of fear, hunger and loss — pointing Muslims towards patience and accountability.

glossary_terms.definition: The Islamic doctrine of predestination: the belief that Allah has foreknowledge of all events and that His divine plan encompasses everything that exists.
In Islamic theology, the divine attributes of Allah, including His eternal foreknowledge of all events and all human choices.
The capacity of human beings to make genuine choices and be held accountable for them, which Muslims believe coexists with Allah's foreknowledge.
A school of Islamic rational theology that strongly emphasised human free will and reason, arguing that Allah cannot compel human sin because that would contradict His justice.
The mainstream school of Sunni theology founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, which holds that Allah has foreknowledge and power over all things while humans 'acquire' responsibility for their actions.
The Islamic concept of the afterlife — the eternal existence that follows death and the Day of Judgement.
The Islamic principle that human beings are trustees of Allah's creation, responsible for acting justly and sustainably on earth.
The intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgement in Islamic belief, sometimes described as a barrier or partition separating the dead from the living.
The Islamic term for paradise or heaven — the eternal reward of the righteous after the Day of Judgement.
The Islamic term for hell or the fire — the place of punishment for those who rejected Allah and committed grave sins without repentance.
One who dies in the path of Allah; in Islamic theology, martyrs are believed to bypass Barzakh and enter paradise immediately.
